builder_plan.scenario: An agent looks good in demos, but you cannot tell which product tasks it fails.
builder_plan.change: Use the study's evaluation idea to inspect a small set of tasks with human-checked answers.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current evaluator and a manually reviewed reference set.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Agreement with human review, missed failures, false alarms, and evaluation cost per task.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Controlling the Probability of Unknown Unknowns in Pre-Deployment Testing of AI Systems
summary: The method replaces heuristic or fixed-horizon Good-Turing stopping rules with an anytime-valid upper confidence sequence for the probability of observing an unseen failure mode. Its cost is additional statistical machinery, dependence on repeated test execution and labeling, and more complex decision logic than a single final evaluation. It can fail if automated failure labels are biased or inconsistent, if the test distribution shifts from deployment, or if the assumed sampling and confidence conditions are violated.
rationale: The reader can apply it to pre-deployment agent evaluation without large infrastructure, but the practical benefit depends on whether their test pipeline supports repeated sampling, reliable failure labeling, and distribution assumptions close enough to production.
technique: Anytime-valid certification of unseen failure probability

claims.statement: The method replaces heuristic or fixed-horizon Good-Turing stopping rules with an anytime-valid upper confidence sequence for the probability of observing an unseen failure mode. Its cost is additional statistical machinery, dependence on repeated test execution and labeling, and more complex decision logic than a single final evaluation. It can fail if automated failure labels are biased or inconsistent, if the test distribution shifts from deployment, or if the assumed sampling and confidence conditions are violated.

On SWE-Chat, the method achieves tighter upper bounds than a multiple-testing corrected Good-Turing baseline and dominates a fixed-horizon Good-Turing upper confidence bound that is not anytime valid.
